news.content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 19-Oct-2026 Hantavirus and the mouth: Review maps early oral warning signs, salivary clues, and precautions for dental teams Oral signs, salivary diagnostics, and dental safety in hantavirus infection Peer-Reviewed Publication Chinese Medical Journals Publishing House Co., Ltd. Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: (1) Andes virus (ANDV) infects the secretory cells of human salivary glands and is shed into saliva. (2) Natural antimicrobials in saliva (histatins, lactoferrin, lysozyme, and SLPI) inactivate Puumala and Hantaan viruses, but ANDV resists them and remains infectious. Salivary mucins MUC5B and MUC7 may help protect the oral surface, and salivary secretory IgA rises sharply in infected patients. (3) Together, these findings offer a biological explanation for why ANDV, alone among hantaviruses, can spread from person to person through deep kissing and close contact in households and healthcare settings. Steps 1 and 2 are based on experimental data; step 3 is a plausible mechanism supported by epidemiological association, not proof that saliva is the route of transmission. view more Credit: Anil, Vishnupriya K. Sweety, Aman Pratap Singh/Infectious Diseases & Immunity Hantaviruses are carried by rodents and cause two serious illnesses in people: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), with an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 cases each year, mostly in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas, which kills up to 40% of those affected. The infections returned to the headlines in May 2026, when the World Health Organization reported a cluster of Andes virus infections linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius: 13 cases and 3 deaths, with more than 600 contacts traced across 32 countries, territories, and areas. Although the effects of hantaviruses on the kidneys, lungs, and blood are well described, the oral and salivary side of infection has received little attention. In an invited review published in Infectious Diseases & Immunity, Prof. Sukumaran Anil of Chulalongkorn University, Thailand, and Manipal Academy of Higher Education, India, with Dr. Vishnupriya K. Sweety and Dr. Aman Pratap Singh, brings together the virology, epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of human hantavirus infection and examines what each means for the mouth and for dental care. Saliva and the one hantavirus that spreads between people Andes virus (ANDV), found in Argentina and Chile, is the only hantavirus for which person-to-person spread has been repeatedly documented, with deep kissing and sexual contact identified as risk factors. The review highlights laboratory evidence that ANDV antigen is present in the secretory cells of human salivary glands and that ANDV, unlike other hantaviruses, resists the natural antiviral activity of human saliva. In a Chilean study of 131 confirmed cases, viral RNA was detected in 30% of acute-phase gingival crevicular fluid (the fluid around the gums) sample and in 12% of acute-phase saliva samples, and replication-competent virus was recovered from 18 of 43 positive samples tested (42%). The authors stress that this makes an oral route biologically plausible but does not prove that saliva carries the infection from one person to another. Warning signs in the mouth A severe sore throat lasting 2 to 3 weeks, together with swelling of the face, neck, and throat, has been described early in hantavirus infection and is easily mistaken for ordinary pharyngitis or tonsillitis. Small hemorrhages on the soft palate may appear during the febrile phase of HFRS. In the later oliguric phase, platelet counts can fall below 20,000-30,000 per microliter, bringing a real risk of spontaneous gum bleeding and of bleeding after even minor oral procedures. Saliva as a diagnostic sample An oral fluid IgM test for Hantaan virus agreed closely with serum testing, with 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity. Because dental clinics handle saliva routinely, the authors propose that dental clinics be evaluated as sites for non-invasive surveillance in endemic communities, while cautioning that the test has not yet been validated in dental patients, in ANDV-endemic populations, or as a point-of-care device. What dental teams can do The review sets out a four-step approach: recognize, time the care, protect the team, and support the patient. Elective dental treatment should be deferred during active illness and resumed only after platelet and kidney function have recovered, in consultation with the treating physician. Unavoidable emergency procedures belong in a hospital setting with support to control bleeding. For suspected HCPS, FFP2 or N95 respirators and hand instruments are preferred over aerosol-generating equipment; for suspected ANDV infection, enhanced protective equipment and a pre-procedural mouthrinse are reasonable precautions. Patients treated with ribavirin may need help with mouth ulcers, taste changes, and dry mouth. The authors are explicit about the limits of the evidence. There are no clinical studies of dental care in hantavirus infection and no reported transmission to a dental worker, so the dental recommendations are precautionary and extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence. Dentists are not expected to diagnose the disease; their role is to avoid dismissing these signs as routine and to refer promptly. “The dentist is unlikely to be the clinician who diagnoses hantavirus infection, but may be the first to notice that a sore throat has lasted far too long or that the gums are bleeding without explanation,” said Prof. Anil. “The cruise ship cluster showed that travel can carry this risk well beyond endemic regions, so every dental team should know these signs and when to refer.” The authors call for prospective studies that document oral findings systematically, longitudinal studies of salivary mucins and immunity, and validation of saliva-based tests in real-world and dental settings. Dentists are not expected to diagnose the disease; their role is to avoid dismissing these signs as routine and to refer promptly. “The dentist is unlikely to be the clinician who diagnoses hantavirus infection, but may be the first to notice that a sore throat has lasted far too long or that the gums are bleeding without explanation,” said Prof. Anil. “The cruise ship cluster showed that travel can carry this risk well beyond endemic regions, so every dental team should know these signs and when to refer.” The authors call for prospective studies that document oral findings systematically, longitudinal studies of salivary mucins and immunity, and validation of saliva-based tests in real-world and dental settings. news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 19 日发表在《传染病与免疫》杂志上的一篇评论文章探讨了汉坦病毒感染的口腔和唾液方面,重点关注安第斯病毒 (ANDV),这是已知的唯一一种通过深吻和密切接触在人与人之间传播的 汉坦病毒。该研究强调,ANDV 感染人类唾液腺并抵抗唾液中的天然 抗病毒药物 活性,使其成为 传播 的潜在 媒介。它还概述了汉坦病毒感染的临床影响,例如长期喉咙痛、面部肿胀和牙龈出血,这些可能被误认为是常见病症。该审查表明,由于唾液的常规处理,牙科诊所可以作为非侵入性 监测 的场所,但警告说,基于唾液的测试尚未在牙科环境中得到验证。作者提出了牙科团队的预防措施,包括加强防护设备和漱口水,并强调需要进一步研究来记录口腔检查结果并验证诊断方法。2026 年 5 月发生的游轮事件涉及 32 个国家的 13 例病例和 3 人死亡,凸显了 ANDV 在全球的传播以及牙科专业人员识别这些迹象并及时转诊患者的重要性。

Concierge Medicine Forum| MGMA 2026| Malpractice Advertisement News|Articles|May 5, 2026 Texas physician convicted for illegally distributing more than a million pills; semaglutide cuts heavy drinking; hantavirus kills three on Atlantic cruise ship – Morning Medical Update Author(s)Austin Littrell Fact checked by: Keith A. Reynolds Listen 0:00 / 4:07 Key Takeaways A federal jury found Barbara Marino, MD guilty of conspiracy and distribution after prescribing >1 million oxycodone, hydrocodone, and carisoprodol pills without legitimate medical purpose. Prosecutors described systematic co-prescribing of opioid–carisoprodol “cocktails” to >99% of patients, typically at the strongest short-acting doses, with patient recruitment by street-level dealers. Weekly semaglutide plus CBT produced a 41.1% reduction in heavy drinking days, outperforming placebo by 13.7 percentage points, with biomarker corroboration and mild, transient gastrointestinal toxicity. Hantavirus exposure typically follows aerosolization of dried rodent urine/droppings; pulmonary syndrome carries ~40% fatality, early influenza-like symptoms delay diagnosis, and treatment remains supportive with possible ventilation. WHO assessed low population-level risk from the cruise-ship cluster, with one confirmed British case and multiple investigations ongoing. SHOW MORE The top news stories in medicine today. Advertisement Morning Medical Update © batuhan toker - stock.adobe.com Texas physician convicted for running pill mill out of cash-only Houston strip mall Barbara Marino, M.D., prescribed opioids to ‘almost every patient she saw,’ including a woman in her third trimester of pregnancy. A federal jury has convicted a Texas physician for unlawfully distributing more than a million pills of oxycodone, hydrocodone and the muscle relaxer carisoprodol from a cash-only clinic in a Houston strip mall. Barbara Marino, MD, 65, of Tomball, was the sole prescribing physician at Angels Clinica, where street-level drug dealers brought patients in exchange for prescriptions that were then filled at local pharmacies and resold on the street. Prosecutors said Marino prescribed the dangerous combination of an opioid and carisoprodol to more than 99% of her patients, almost always in the strongest short-acting doses available and received more than $400,000 in less than a year for writing prescriptions that lacked a legitimate medical purpose. Among her patients was a woman in her third trimester of pregnancy, whose OB/GYN testified at trial about the dangers of the drug cocktail Marino prescribed her. Marino was convicted of one count of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance and four counts of distributing a controlled substance, each carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up GLP-1s reduce heavy drinking A clinical trial found weekly semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days by 41% in patients with obesity and alcohol use disorder. Weekly injections of semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days by 41.1% in patients with alcohol use disorder and obesity — a 13.7 percentage point greater reduction than placebo — according to the first randomized controlled trial to test a GLP-1 receptor agonist specifically in this population, published in The Lancet. The 26-week trial, led by researchers at Copenhagen University Hospital with National Institutes of Health (NIH) collaboration, enrolled 108 treatment-seeking patients who received either semaglutide or placebo alongside standard cognitive behavioral therapy. Blood-alcohol biomarkers supported the self-reported drinking data, and the drug's number needed to treat was 4.3, comparing favorably to approved alcohol use disorder medications, which generally require treating seven or more patients to see one benefit. Side effects were mild and transient, primarily gastrointestinal. "Very few medications are currently approved for alcohol use disorder, and these are vastly underutilized," said NIAAA Director George Koob, Ph.D., a study co-author. Larger and longer trials are needed to confirm the findings. What is Hantavirus? The virus killed 3 aboard an Atlantic cruise ship Three passengers died and several others fell ill aboard the MV Hondius, an Atlantic cruise ship, in a suspected outbreak of the rare rodent-borne virus. A suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a Dutch cruise ship, the MV Hondius, has killed three passengers and left several others ill. Hantavirus is a family of rodent-borne viruses most commonly contracted when dried droppings, urine or saliva from infected animals become airborne — typically during cleaning or disturbing areas where rodents have nested. The virus causes two syndromes: hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, the respiratory form most common in North and South America, carries a fatality rate of roughly 40%; the other primarily attacks the kidneys. Early symptoms resemble influenza and appear one to eight weeks after exposure, making diagnosis in the first 72 hours difficult; respiratory deterioration can follow rapidly. There is no specific antiviral treatment, care is supportive and severe cases may require mechanical ventilation. Person-to-person transmission is rare. The World Health Organization (WHO) said the risk to the general public remains low, with one confirmed case identified in a British passenger hospitalized in South Africa and five others under investigation. Concierge Medicine Forum| MGMA 2026| Malpractice Advertisement News|Articles|May 5, 2026 Texas physician convicted for illegally distributing more than a million pills; semaglutide cuts heavy drinking; hantavirus kills three on Atlantic cruise ship – Morning Medical Update Author(s)Austin Littrell Fact checked by: Keith A. Reynolds Listen 0:00 / 4:07 Key Takeaways A federal jury found Barbara Marino, MD guilty of conspiracy and distribution after prescribing >1 million oxycodone, hydrocodone, and carisoprodol pills without legitimate medical purpose. Prosecutors described systematic co-prescribing of opioid–carisoprodol “cocktails” to >99% of patients, typically at the strongest short-acting doses, with patient recruitment by street-level dealers. Weekly semaglutide plus CBT produced a 41.1% reduction in heavy drinking days, outperforming placebo by 13.7 percentage points, with biomarker corroboration and mild, transient gastrointestinal toxicity. Hantavirus exposure typically follows aerosolization of dried rodent urine/droppings; pulmonary syndrome carries ~40% fatality, early influenza-like symptoms delay diagnosis, and treatment remains supportive with possible ventilation. WHO assessed low population-level risk from the cruise-ship cluster, with one confirmed British case and multiple investigations ongoing. SHOW MORE The top news stories in medicine today. Advertisement Morning Medical Update © batuhan toker - stock.adobe.com Texas physician convicted for running pill mill out of cash-only Houston strip mall Barbara Marino, M.D., prescribed opioids to ‘almost every patient she saw,’ including a woman in her third trimester of pregnancy. A federal jury has convicted a Texas physician for unlawfully distributing more than a million pills of oxycodone, hydrocodone and the muscle relaxer carisoprodol from a cash-only clinic in a Houston strip mall. Barbara Marino, MD, 65, of Tomball, was the sole prescribing physician at Angels Clinica, where street-level drug dealers brought patients in exchange for prescriptions that were then filled at local pharmacies and resold on the street. Prosecutors said Marino prescribed the dangerous combination of an opioid and carisoprodol to more than 99% of her patients, almost always in the strongest short-acting doses available and received more than $400,000 in less than a year for writing prescriptions that lacked a legitimate medical purpose. Among her patients was a woman in her third trimester of pregnancy, whose OB/GYN testified at trial about the dangers of the drug cocktail Marino prescribed her. Marino was convicted of one count of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance and four counts of distributing a controlled substance, each carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up GLP-1s reduce heavy drinking A clinical trial found weekly semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days by 41% in patients with obesity and alcohol use disorder. Weekly injections of semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days by 41.1% in patients with alcohol use disorder and obesity — a 13.7 percentage point greater reduction than placebo — according to the first randomized controlled trial to test a GLP-1 receptor agonist specifically in this population, published in The Lancet. The 26-week trial, led by researchers at Copenhagen University Hospital with National Institutes of Health (NIH) collaboration, enrolled 108 treatment-seeking patients who received either semaglutide or placebo alongside standard cognitive behavioral therapy. Blood-alcohol biomarkers supported the self-reported drinking data, and the drug's number needed to treat was 4.3, comparing favorably to approved alcohol use disorder medications, which generally require treating seven or more patients to see one benefit. Side effects were mild and transient, primarily gastrointestinal. "Very few medications are currently approved for alcohol use disorder, and these are vastly underutilized," said NIAAA Director George Koob, Ph.D., a study co-author. Larger and longer trials are needed to confirm the findings. What is Hantavirus? The virus killed 3 aboard an Atlantic cruise ship Three passengers died and several others fell ill aboard the MV Hondius, an Atlantic cruise ship, in a suspected outbreak of the rare rodent-borne virus. A suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a Dutch cruise ship, the MV Hondius, has killed three passengers and left several others ill. Hantavirus is a family of rodent-borne viruses most commonly contracted when dried droppings, urine or saliva from infected animals become airborne — typically during cleaning or disturbing areas where rodents have nested. The virus causes two syndromes: hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, the respiratory form most common in North and South America, carries a fatality rate of roughly 40%; the other primarily attacks the kidneys. Early symptoms resemble influenza and appear one to eight weeks after exposure, making diagnosis in the first 72 hours difficult; respiratory deterioration can follow rapidly. There is no specific antiviral treatment, care is supportive and severe cases may require mechanical ventilation. Person-to-person transmission is rare. The World Health Organization (WHO) said the risk to the general public remains low, with one confirmed case identified in a British passenger hospitalized in South Africa and five others under investigation. Concierge Medicine Forum| MGMA 2026| Malpractice Advertisement News|Articles|May 21, 2026 Physicians say hantavirus headlines outpace actual risk; three sentenced in Moscow-based $2B telemedicine fraud; 1 in 10 surgeons leave the profession within 8 years – Morning Medical Update Author(s)Austin Littrell Fact checked by: Keith A. Reynolds Listen 0:00 / 4:14 Key Takeaways Surveyed clinicians reported 85% perceived hantavirus coverage as exaggerated, while 77% rated population risk low/non-meaningful and 62% observed increased patient questions. Most management centered on counseling: 89% prioritized explaining transmission, alongside reassurance about limited person-to-person spread and guidance to reduce rodent exposure. Federal sentencing addressed a 2017–2022 scheme using call centers, ghost telehealth encounters, and remotely controlled pharmacies across 75+ sites to generate prescriptions irrespective of consent. Insurers paid >$758M on $1.97B in claims; operators used aliases, shell entities, encrypted communications, straw owners, and international laundering, with an alleged leader still abroad. Longitudinal surgeon data showed near-10% eight-year attrition, peaking in 2020; mid-career departures were greatest, rural representation fell 10.5% to 8.5%, and female share rose to 28.6%. SHOW MORE The top news stories in medicine today. Advertisement Morning Medical Update © Alena Kryazheva – stock.adobe.com Physicians say hantavirus media coverage is outpacing the actual risk A Sermo survey of 104 doctors found 85% believe current coverage exaggerates the public threat, even as 62% report a rise in patient inquiries. More than eight in ten physicians say media coverage of hantavirus is overstating the actual risk to the general public, even as patient anxiety climbs in the wake of recent headlines, according to a new Sermo survey of 104 U.S. physicians across infectious disease, internal medicine, pulmonology and emergency medicine. Seventy-seven percent of respondents rated the current risk to the general public as low or non-meaningful, consistent with CDC data showing fewer than 50 hantavirus cases are typically reported in the U.S. annually. Yet 62% of physicians said they have already seen an increase in patient inquiries about the virus. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up Physicians described a familiar dynamic: heightened media coverage driving patient concern without a corresponding change in underlying disease risk. The most common clinical response was education on transmission, cited by 89% of respondents, followed by reassurance about low transmission risk and prevention guidance around rodent exposure. Three sentenced in Moscow-based $2B telemedicine fraud scheme targeting U.S. insurers The criminal organization ran ghost telemedicine visits, fraudulent prescriptions and remotely controlled pharmacies across more than 75 locations nationwide. Three members of a Moscow-based criminal organization have been sentenced to federal prison for their roles in a nearly $2 billion health care fraud conspiracy that used sham telemedicine visits, fraudulent prescriptions and remotely operated pharmacies to defraud private insurers, with many patients never receiving the medications billed in their names. Anthony Santamaria received 10 years; co-defendants Hershel Tsikman and Hafizullah Ebady received 120 and 97 months, respectively. Between 2017 and 2022, the organization used call centers in Utah and later Russia to contact insurance beneficiaries and generate prescriptions regardless of whether they agreed to receive medications, then submitted more than $1.97 billion in fraudulent claims through over 75 pharmacies acquired across New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan and Alabama. Private insurers paid out more than $758 million before the scheme was uncovered. The defendants concealed their involvement through aliases, encrypted communications, shell companies and straw owners, laundering proceeds internationally. The organization's alleged leader, U.S. citizen Brian Sutton, is believed to be living abroad and remains at large. Three additional co-defendants are awaiting sentencing. Nearly 1 in 10 surgeons leave the profession within 8 years, study finds Mid-career surgeons are most at risk, and attrition spiked sharply in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Nearly 10% of surgeons left clinical practice within an eight-year period, with attrition highest among mid-career surgeons and in subspecialties including oral and maxillofacial surgery, obstetrics and gynecology, and plastic and reconstructive surgery, according to a new study published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons. Researchers at Ohio State University analyzed data on more than 224,000 surgeons across 19 specialties from 2013 to 2023 and found overall attrition rates held steady until 2020, when they rose sharply, likely driven by pandemic-era retirements. Five-year cumulative attrition was highest in oral and maxillofacial surgery at 25.1%, followed by obstetrics and gynecology at 23.2% and plastic and reconstructive surgery at 19.3%. The share of surgeons practicing in rural areas shrank from 10.5% to 8.5% over the decade, while the percentage of female surgeons rose from 21.2% to 28.6%. "Surgical attrition is a real problem, and we need to address it in a nuanced and tailored way," said co-author Timothy Pawlik, M.D., M.P.H., Ph.D., FACS, of Ohio State's Wexner Medical Center. OffOn Stream on News American speaks out from cruise ship amid deadly hantavirus outbreak American passenger speaks out after suspected hantavirus outbreak on cruise ship ByKelly McCarthy May 5, 2026, 6:54 PM An American passenger aboard a luxury cruise ship at the center of a deadly suspected hantavirus outbreak is speaking out on social media about the ongoing situation. "There's a lot of uncertainty, and that's the hardest part," passenger Jake Rosmarin said in a video posted to Instagram from the MV Hondius. "All we want right now is to feel safe, to have clarity, and to get home." Oceanwide Expeditions, the cruise ship's Netherlands-based operator, said in its latest update on Monday that medical crews are working to evacuate sick passengers from the ship, which is currently anchored off Cape Verde. Rosmarin is one of 149 people onboard the ship, representing 23 different nationalities, Oceanwide Expeditions said in a press release. This aerial picture shows a general view of the cruise ship MV Hondius stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 4, 2026. AFP via Getty Images "What's happening right now is very real for all of us here. We're not just a story. We're not just headlines. We're people. People with families, with lives, with people waiting for us at home," Rosmarin said. The ship left from Argentina three weeks ago, originally bound for Antarctica. South African health officials said in a press release Monday that some passengers began experiencing "serious health complications arising from what was initially considered severe acute respiratory infections." The first two deaths were a married couple from the Netherlands, according to Oceanwide Expeditions. The 70-year-old male passenger became ill first with a fever, headache, abdominal pain, and diarrhea starting on April 6. He died onboard on April 11, the cruise operator said. The cause of death was not determined onboard, it added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know No microbiological tests were performed at the time, according to the World Health Organization. WHO said the man's wife fell ill on the subsequent repatriation flight to Johannesburg and died in the emergency department two weeks later. Testing later confirmed the woman was infected with hantavirus. Contact tracing for passengers on that flight has since been initiated, according to WHO officials. Popular Reads Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search 1 day ago Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress 1 day ago Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Oct 16 A third passenger, a British national, fell ill on April 24 and was medically evacuated to South Africa, where he remains hospitalized in an intensive care unit, WHO stated. Health officials said the man's laboratory test results came back positive for hantavirus. A fourth passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to WHO officials. The woman later died on May 2. Oceanwide Expeditions said the cause of death has not yet been established. Related The tragic deaths of Gene Hackman and Betsy Arakawa: A timeline Cruise passengers have been told to stay in their cabins and practice strict hygiene protocols. The cruise line said disembarkation, medical evacuation or medical screening requires permission from and coordination with local and international health authorities. Hantaviruses are a family of viruses that can cause serious illnesses and death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Humans can contract hantavirus through contact with rodents including rats and mice, "especially when exposed to their urine, droppings, and saliva," the CDC states. "There have been reported cases of human-to-human transmission of one of the hantavirus species, which is found in Argentina, so I think that that is part of the decision as well as the timeline that is emerging for asking the passengers to quarantine," Dr. Emily Abdoler, a clinical associate professor of medicine at the University of Michigan told ABC News. In a statement Tuesday, Oceanwide Expeditions said, "The medical evacuation of two individuals currently requiring urgent medical care, and the individual associated with the guest who passed away on 2 May, will occur using two specialized aircraft that are en route to Cape Verde. From here, the patients are to be medically evacuated to the Netherlands. At this stage, we do not have an exact timeline." The cruise operator added that once the individuals had been "safely transferred from the vessel and are in transit to the Netherlands," the shop would begin repositioning. "Our plan is to proceed to the Canary Islands, either Gran Canaria or Tenerife, which will take 3 days of sailing," it said. "Discussions are ongoing with relevant authorities. This will be shared when concrete plans are available." Ângela Gomes, national director of health of Cape Verde, said in a statement Tuesday that a regional hospital has "prepared an area with isolation capacity, should it be necessary" moving forward. "A dedicated team has been formed, with doctors, infectious disease specialists, nurses and laboratory technicians, to support patients on board and, if necessary, also on land," Gomes added. analysis.event: A suspected hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship, with confirmed cases and deaths; reported by an American passenger and Oceanwide Expeditions.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: At least four confirmed cases, two deaths (a married couple from the Netherlands), and one hospitalized in intensive care; health officials are conducting contact tracing and medical evacuations.

analysis.brief_en: An American passenger aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, anchored off Cape Verde, has spoken out about a suspected hantavirus outbreak affecting 149 people from 23 nationalities. The outbreak has led to at least four confirmed cases, with two deaths reported: a 70-year-old Dutch man who died onboard on April 11 and his wife, who succumbed to the illness two weeks later in South Africa. A British passenger fell ill on April 24 and was hospitalized in intensive care, while a German woman developed pneumonia symptoms and died on May 2. Oceanwide Expeditions, the cruise operator, has initiated medical evacuations and is coordinating with health authorities for disembarkation and further actions. The World Health Organization confirmed the infection in the Dutch woman and is conducting contact tracing. The cause of death for the Dutch man remains undetermined, and no microbiological tests were initially performed. Hantaviruses, which can cause severe illnesses and death, are typically transmitted through rodent contact, though human-to-human transmission has been reported in some cases. The cruise line plans to reposition to the Canary Islands after medical evacuations are completed.

The outbreak has led to at least four confirmed cases, with two deaths reported: a 70-year-old Dutch man who died onboard on April 11 and his wife, who succumbed to the illness two weeks later in South Africa. A British passenger fell ill on April 24 and was hospitalized in intensive care, while a German woman developed pneumonia symptoms and died on May 2. Oceanwide Expeditions, the cruise operator, has initiated medical evacuations and is coordinating with health authorities for disembarkation and further actions. The World Health Organization confirmed the infection in the Dutch woman and is conducting contact tracing. The cause of death for the Dutch man remains undetermined, and no microbiological tests were initially performed. Hantaviruses, which can cause severe illnesses and death, are typically transmitted through rodent contact, though human-to-human transmission has been reported in some cases. The cruise line plans to reposition to the Canary Islands after medical evacuations are completed.

news.source_body_en: An American passenger aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, anchored off Cape Verde, has spoken out about a suspected hantavirus outbreak affecting 149 people from 23 nationalities. The outbreak has led to at least four confirmed cases, with two deaths reported: a 70-year-old Dutch man who died onboard on April 11 and his wife, who succumbed to the illness two weeks later in South Africa. A British passenger fell ill on April 24 and was hospitalized in intensive care, while a German woman developed pneumonia symptoms and died on May 2. Oceanwide Expeditions, the cruise operator, has initiated medical evacuations and is coordinating with health authorities for disembarkation and further actions. The World Health Organization confirmed the infection in the Dutch woman and is conducting contact tracing. The cause of death for the Dutch man remains undetermined, and no microbiological tests were initially performed. Hantaviruses, which can cause severe illnesses and death, are typically transmitted through rodent contact, though human-to-human transmission has been reported in some cases. The cruise line plans to reposition to the Canary Islands after medical evacuations are completed.
news.content_zh: 停泊在佛得角附近的 MV Hondius 游轮上的一名美国乘客讲述了疑似汉坦病毒暴发 事件,影响了来自 23 个国家的 149 人。暴发 号已导致至少 4 例确诊病例,其中 2 例死亡:一名 70 岁荷兰男子于 4 月 11 日在船上死亡,他的妻子两周后在南非去世。一名英国乘客于 4 月 24 日生病并在重症监护室住院,而一名德国妇女出现肺炎症状并于 5 月 2 日死亡。邮轮运营商 Oceanwide Expeditions 已启动医疗疏散,并正在与卫生当局协调下船和采取进一步行动。世界卫生组织确认了这名荷兰妇女的感染情况,并正在进行接触者追踪。这名荷兰男子的死因仍未确定,最初也没有进行微生物检测。汉坦病毒可导致严重疾病和死亡,通常通过啮齿动物接触传播,但在某些情况下也有人传人的 传播 报道。该邮轮公司计划在医疗后送完成后重新定位到加那利群岛。

news.content_title: Hantavirus spike structure reveals recessed protocadherin-1 binding pocket
news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hantavirus spike structure reveals recessed protocadherin-1 binding pocket by October 22, 2026 in Health, Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hantavirus spike structure reveals recessed protocadherin-1 binding pocket Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The assembled spike of Andes virus uses four glycoproteins to form a deep central pocket that captures protocadherin-1, according to a structural and functional study of hantavirus receptor recognition. Cryo-electron microscopy showed at near-atomic resolution that the membrane-distal extracellular cadherin domain of human protocadherin-1, or PCDH1, inserts asymmetrically into a cavity created by four Gn glycoproteins in the viral spike. The structure explains why PCDH1 can bind assembled viral particles and soluble spike tetramers but not isolated glycoproteins, and it identifies the molecular features that allow New World hantaviruses to recognize the receptor. The study also found that four human neutralizing antibodies block PCDH1 engagement through two distinct mechanisms: direct occlusion of the pocket and steric interference from antibody constant regions. Its envelope contains a spike complex made from the glycoprotein Gn, which forms the receptor-binding head, and Gc, the fusion protein. For the principal structural experiment, the investigators expressed a soluble, tetrameric Andes virus spike together with the extracellular EC1–EC4 region of human PCDH1. The resulting cryo-electron microscopy structure placed one PCDH1 EC1 domain inside a central cavity formed by four Gn molecules. Contacts through the receptor’s BC and FG loops anchored PCDH1 within the pocket, while the geometry of the assembled spike determined whether the receptor could be engaged. That quaternary architecture makes hantavirus receptor recognition dependent on the organization of multiple viral proteins rather than a single linear binding site. Discover more Try Science Kits Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Earth An isolated Gn glycoprotein does not reproduce the surface created when four Gn subunits converge around the spike axis. The findings therefore provide a structural explanation for the observed preference of PCDH1 for intact viral particles or soluble spike tetramers over soluble glycoproteins. The pocket can be compared with receptor-binding sites in alphaviruses that likewise arise only after glycoprotein assembly. The molecular arrangements are different, however: the EC1 domain of protocadherin-10 binds the western equine encephalitis virus spike laterally through its A, G, F and C beta strands, whereas PCDH1 enters the hantavirus pocket axially through BC and FG loops. The comparison shows that related non-clustered delta-cadherin receptors can use distinctly shaped surfaces on enveloped-virus glycoproteins. The receptor’s own organization adds another layer to the interaction. PCDH1 is a calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion protein whose soluble ectodomain fragments can exist in a monomer–dimer equilibrium. Previous structural work showed that PCDH1 can form antiparallel homodimers through an EC1–EC4 interface, but the oligomeric distribution of full-length PCDH1 at the plasma membrane has not been established. The receptor configuration captured in the Andes virus complex is incompatible with that stable antiparallel arrangement because the EC4 domain would not fit into the viral cavity. Recombinant PCDH1 mutants engineered to remain monomeric did not reduce binding to a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus displaying the Andes virus spike, whereas stabilizing PCDH1 dimers increased binding. Together, these observations suggest that Andes virus primarily engages monomeric PCDH1 at the cell surface, while transiently exposed EC1 domains on dynamic receptors might also contribute. Mutagenesis and sequence analysis identified three Gn loops—the AB, CD and DE loops—that help shape the PCDH1-binding surface. Discover more Earth’s Health Biology Study Biology Order DNA Kits Deep mutational scanning of the Andes virus Gn ectodomain found that substitutions in the CD and AB loops can alter affinity for PCDH1. The CD loop was particularly flexible, variable and tolerant of multiple mutations, making it a plausible point of variation during adaptation. The four-subunit pocket could also permit a limited number of amino acid substitutions, distributed among its component Gn molecules, to influence receptor recognition. These are observations from laboratory mutagenesis and viral systems; they do not establish a particular evolutionary pathway in circulating hantaviruses or show that any specific population has acquired a new receptor. Loop-transfer experiments tested whether receptor specificity could be shifted between New World and Old World hantavirus glycoproteins. In recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying different hantavirus Gn–Gc combinations, transferring the Andes virus CD loop into the corresponding glycoprotein of Sin Nombre virus or hantavirus Taira virus enabled substantial PCDH1 recognition. Constructs carrying all three receptor-interacting loops produced a similar result, while the CD loop alone was sufficient in the tested systems. The result identifies sequence variation in Gn as a major determinant of PCDH1 recognition. It does not show that either Old World virus naturally binds PCDH1 or that one has begun evolving toward that behavior. Structural and functional analysis of four human neutralizing antibodies demonstrated that the recessed pocket can be blocked in more than one way. ANDV-5 and MIB22 recognized epitopes adjacent to, but outside, the central cavity and directly occluded access to PCDH1. ADI-65534 and ANDV-34 did not directly compete with the receptor. Instead, their antibody constant regions sterically interfered with receptor engagement, allowing them to neutralize the virus by binding an accessible spike surface and preventing PCDH1 from occupying its binding site. The cavity itself is too narrow to accommodate a conventional antibody readily, explaining why the antibodies recognized sites around its rim rather than reaching deeply into the pocket. The separation between the receptor-binding and antibody-binding surfaces suggests a possible route to viral escape. PCDH1 contacts a relatively small and buried interface, whereas an antibody such as MIB22 engages a broader, more exposed surface. Changes that disrupt the larger antibody interface could therefore leave important elements of receptor recognition intact. Consistent with that possibility, Andes virus escape mutations associated with MIB22 occurred at residues distinct from, and more peripheral to, those critical for Andes virus–PCDH1 recognition. The study did not directly test receptor use by an escaped strain, so the structural separation remains a mechanism supported by the combined structural and mutational evidence rather than a demonstrated outcome in natural infections. The receptor pocket may also be relevant to how the spike transitions from attachment to membrane fusion. The PCDH1-binding cavity is formed by Gn and does not involve the fusion protein Gc, suggesting that receptor engagement and membrane fusion might be separate events in hantaviruses. Gn has also been reported to adopt a different tetrameric arrangement at acidic pH, leaving open the possibility that receptor binding could affect fusion activation, although the present structural work does not resolve that question. Antibodies designed to reach conserved residues at the base of the cavity might require unusually long complementarity-determining loops, single-domain antibodies or other biologics engineered for the confined space. Antibodies recognizing epitopes that are partly buried in the intact spike might alternatively prevent formation of the receptor-binding pocket itself. The findings offer a structural framework for hantavirus antiviral design, but they do not establish a treatment, preventive measure or clinical benefit. The experiments combined cryo-electron microscopy of PCDH1 bound to a soluble Andes virus spike and to virus-like particles, X-ray crystallography of an antibody–glycoprotein complex, mutagenesis, deep mutational scanning, receptor-binding measurements and infection assays using recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses. These systems reproduced selected molecular and entry characteristics of hantaviruses, but the study did not evaluate natural infection in people, human vaccine responses, disease outcomes, or the safety and efficacy of candidate drugs. Atomic coordinates, raw sequencing data and analysis code were deposited in public repositories. By revealing that receptor recognition and antibody neutralization depend on precise three-dimensional relationships within the assembled spike, the work identifies a concentrated target for future molecular design while leaving its clinical translation unproven. Instead, their antibody constant regions sterically interfered with receptor engagement, allowing them to neutralize the virus by binding an accessible spike surface and preventing PCDH1 from occupying its binding site. The cavity itself is too narrow to accommodate a conventional antibody readily, explaining why the antibodies recognized sites around its rim rather than reaching deeply into the pocket. The separation between the receptor-binding and antibody-binding surfaces suggests a possible route to viral escape. PCDH1 contacts a relatively small and buried interface, whereas an antibody such as MIB22 engages a broader, more exposed surface. Changes that disrupt the larger antibody interface could therefore leave important elements of receptor recognition intact. Consistent with that possibility, Andes virus escape mutations associated with MIB22 occurred at residues distinct from, and more peripheral to, those critical for Andes virus–PCDH1 recognition. The study did not directly test receptor use by an escaped strain, so the structural separation remains a mechanism supported by the combined structural and mutational evidence rather than a demonstrated outcome in natural infections. The receptor pocket may also be relevant to how the spike transitions from attachment to membrane fusion. The PCDH1-binding cavity is formed by Gn and does not involve the fusion protein Gc, suggesting that receptor engagement and membrane fusion might be separate events in hantaviruses. Gn has also been reported to adopt a different tetrameric arrangement at acidic pH, leaving open the possibility that receptor binding could affect fusion activation, although the present structural work does not resolve that question. Antibodies designed to reach conserved residues at the base of the cavity might require unusually long complementarity-determining loops, single-domain antibodies or other biologics engineered for the confined space. Antibodies recognizing epitopes that are partly buried in the intact spike might alternatively prevent formation of the receptor-binding pocket itself. The findings offer a structural framework for hantavirus antiviral design, but they do not establish a treatment, preventive measure or clinical benefit. The experiments combined cryo-electron microscopy of PCDH1 bound to a soluble Andes virus spike and to virus-like particles, X-ray crystallography of an antibody–glycoprotein complex, mutagenesis, deep mutational scanning, receptor-binding measurements and infection assays using recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses. These systems reproduced selected molecular and entry characteristics of hantaviruses, but the study did not evaluate natural infection in people, human vaccine responses, disease outcomes, or the safety and efficacy of candidate drugs. Atomic coordinates, raw sequencing data and analysis code were deposited in public repositories. By revealing that receptor recognition and antibody neutralization depend on precise three-dimensional relationships within the assembled spike, the work identifies a concentrated target for future molecular design while leaving its clinical translation unproven. analysis.brief_en: A recent study published on October 22, 2026, by Bioengineer.org investigated the structural and functional aspects of hantavirus receptor recognition. The research focused on the Andes virus, revealing that its spike complex forms a deep central pocket using four glycoproteins to capture protocadherin-1 (PCDH1). Cryo-electron microscopy showed that the PCDH1 extracellular domain inserts asymmetrically into this cavity, and the study identified molecular features enabling New World hantaviruses to recognize the receptor. It also found that four human neutralizing antibodies block PCDH1 engagement through two mechanisms: direct occlusion of the pocket and steric interference. The findings suggest that the receptor configuration captured in the Andes virus complex is incompatible with a stable antiparallel arrangement of PCDH1, and that sequence variation in the Gn glycoprotein plays a major role in receptor recognition. However, the study does not establish clinical benefits or treatment measures, and the results are based on laboratory experiments rather than field observations.

news.content_zh: Bioengineer.org 于 2026 年 10 月 22 日发表的一项最新研究调查了汉坦病毒受体识别的结构和功能方面。该研究重点关注安第斯山脉病毒,揭示其刺突复合物使用四种糖蛋白形成一个深中央口袋来捕获原钙粘蛋白-1 (PCDH1)。冷冻电子显微镜显示 PCDH1 胞外结构域不对称地插入到该腔中,并且该研究确定了使 New World汉坦病毒能够识别该受体的分子特征。它还发现四种人类中和抗体通过两种机制阻断 PCDH1 的结合:口袋的直接闭塞和空间干扰。研究结果表明,安第斯病毒复合体中捕获的受体构型与 PCDH1 的稳定反平行排列不相容,并且 Gn 糖蛋白的序列变异在受体识别中发挥着重要作用。然而,该研究没有建立临床效益或 治疗 措施,并且结果基于实验室实验而不是现场观察。

OffOn Stream on WHO says suspected hantavirus cluster 'is not the start of a COVID pandemic' There are 12 suspected cases so far. ByMary Kekatos and Zoe Magee May 7, 2026, 4:39 PM An epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that the suspected hantavirus cluster aboard a cruise ship is not the beginning of another COVID-19 pandemic. Eight cases are currently being reported by the WHO, including five laboratory-confirmed cases and three suspected cases. Of those eight cases, three have died. Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, an infectious disease epidemiologist and acting director of epidemic and pandemic management at the WHO, was asked during a press conference what the difference was between this cluster and the early days of the COVID pandemic. Related Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US "I want to be unequivocal here. This is not SARS-CoV-2. This is not the start of a COVID pandemic. This is an outbreak that we see on a ship," Van Kerkhove said. Van Kerkhove explained that hantavirus doesn't spread in the same way that coronaviruses do, but rather through "close, intimate contact." Most hantaviruses don't transmit from person to person. "The actions that are being taken on board [the ship] are precautionary to prevent any onward spread," she added. Health personnel assisting patients onto a boat from the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images There appears to be two confirmed cases and four suspected cases that have not been added to the WHO's official count yet. The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport confirmed that two patients infected with the virus are currently hospitalized in the Netherlands, one at Radboud University Medical Center and the other at Leiden University Medical Center. Additionally, two Singapore residents who were on board the ship are currently being monitored. Singapore's Communicable Diseases Agency said it was notified of the individuals on May 4 and 5. "They have been isolated at the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, where they are being tested for hantavirus. The risk to the general public in Singapore is currently low," the agency said. The agency added that test results are pending, with one resident having a runny nose. The other is asymptomatic. The French Health Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday that a French national has been tested after they displayed mild symptoms. This person had been in contact with one of the confirmed cases. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Three deaths have been recorded so far, including a married Dutch couple. The 70-year-old male patient died on April 11, and his body was taken off the ship on the island of St. Helena on April 24. His 69-year-old wife disembarked on the same day, and her health rapidly deteriorated. She died at a South Africa hospital on April 26. A third passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to the WHO. The woman died on May 2 from causes not yet known, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the cruise ship. The WHO said 29 people disembarked on St. Helena on the same day that the body of the Dutch male patient and his wife disembarked. They traveled to 12 countries: Canada, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, Great Britain, St. Kitts and Nevis, Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Sweden, Turkey and the United States. Popular Reads Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search 1 day ago Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress 1 day ago Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Oct 16 The disembarked guests have all been contacted by Oceanwide Expeditions. In the U.S., local authorities in five states -- Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas and Virginia -- are monitoring the disembarked passengers and are conducting contact tracing, None have shown signs of illness at this time. Anais Legend, technical lead for viral hemorrhagic fevers at WHO, said during the press conference on Thursday that "step-by-step guidance is being developed" for the disembarked passengers and that the WHO is coordinating with national authorities. Anyone with any signs of symptoms will be isolated while other passengers have their risk exposure evaluated. The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers suspected of having cases of hantavirus on board, leaves Praia, Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. Reuters Public health experts said they expected a more robust response from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health. "CDC would typically be asked by WHO to, or by a country to, help in technical assistance," Dr. Carlos del Rio, an H. Cliff Sauls distinguished professor of medicine at the Emory University School of Medicine, told reporters on Thursday. Typically, CDC teams would be deployed to an area, he said, and the teams would perform contact tracing and interviews and conduct an outbreak investigation. "I would envision by now, many, many days ago, we would have seen ... a team from CDC deployed to the area," he added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the IDSA, added that she would have expected a CDC press briefing, an alert from the agency's Health Alert Network or information from the NIH on potential treatments in the pipeline that could receive emergency use authorization to help treat hantavirus patients. Marrazzo said she is not aware that conversations about potential therapies at NIH aren't happening but it "does not give me a lot of assurance or reassurance that we're not hearing about any of it." The CDC posted a statement on X on Wednesday on behalf of NIH Director and acting CDC director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that read, "Our hearts go out to the passengers aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius and their families during this difficult time. Our CDC team began coordinating with domestic and international partners as soon as we were notified of a hantavirus situation." The statement said there is "clear, written health guidance to the American passengers through the State Department" and that the CDC "will continue to update as more information becomes available and remains committed to protecting the health and safety of the American public." The agency also published a statement on its website stating that the Trump administration "is closely monitoring the situation" and that the Department of State "is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." The CDC also said the risk to the American public is "extremely low." The WHO said during Thursday's press briefing that the U.S. is coordinating with the global health agency in a technical capacity. Because the cluster is limited and confined to a cruise ship, the "idea of sending messages across the world and panicking everyone is not required," said Dr. Abdirahman Mahmoud, director of the WHO's health emergency alert and response operations. He added that the WHO is "informally" aware that contact tracing has been done of the U.S. passengers who disembarked last month and are back home. OffOn Stream on WHO says suspected hantavirus cluster 'is not the start of a COVID pandemic' There are 12 suspected cases so far. ByMary Kekatos and Zoe Magee May 7, 2026, 4:39 PM An epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that the suspected hantavirus cluster aboard a cruise ship is not the beginning of another COVID-19 pandemic. Eight cases are currently being reported by the WHO, including five laboratory-confirmed cases and three suspected cases. Of those eight cases, three have died. Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, an infectious disease epidemiologist and acting director of epidemic and pandemic management at the WHO, was asked during a press conference what the difference was between this cluster and the early days of the COVID pandemic. Related Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US "I want to be unequivocal here. This is not SARS-CoV-2. This is not the start of a COVID pandemic. This is an outbreak that we see on a ship," Van Kerkhove said. Van Kerkhove explained that hantavirus doesn't spread in the same way that coronaviruses do, but rather through "close, intimate contact." Most hantaviruses don't transmit from person to person. "The actions that are being taken on board [the ship] are precautionary to prevent any onward spread," she added. Health personnel assisting patients onto a boat from the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images There appears to be two confirmed cases and four suspected cases that have not been added to the WHO's official count yet. The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport confirmed that two patients infected with the virus are currently hospitalized in the Netherlands, one at Radboud University Medical Center and the other at Leiden University Medical Center. Additionally, two Singapore residents who were on board the ship are currently being monitored. Singapore's Communicable Diseases Agency said it was notified of the individuals on May 4 and 5. "They have been isolated at the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, where they are being tested for hantavirus. The risk to the general public in Singapore is currently low," the agency said. The agency added that test results are pending, with one resident having a runny nose. The other is asymptomatic. The French Health Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday that a French national has been tested after they displayed mild symptoms. This person had been in contact with one of the confirmed cases. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Three deaths have been recorded so far, including a married Dutch couple. The 70-year-old male patient died on April 11, and his body was taken off the ship on the island of St. Helena on April 24. His 69-year-old wife disembarked on the same day, and her health rapidly deteriorated. She died at a South Africa hospital on April 26. A third passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to the WHO. The woman died on May 2 from causes not yet known, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the cruise ship. The WHO said 29 people disembarked on St. Helena on the same day that the body of the Dutch male patient and his wife disembarked. They traveled to 12 countries: Canada, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, Great Britain, St. Kitts and Nevis, Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Sweden, Turkey and the United States. Popular Reads Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search 1 day ago Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress 1 day ago Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Oct 16 The disembarked guests have all been contacted by Oceanwide Expeditions. In the U.S., local authorities in five states -- Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas and Virginia -- are monitoring the disembarked passengers and are conducting contact tracing, None have shown signs of illness at this time. Anais Legend, technical lead for viral hemorrhagic fevers at WHO, said during the press conference on Thursday that "step-by-step guidance is being developed" for the disembarked passengers and that the WHO is coordinating with national authorities. Anyone with any signs of symptoms will be isolated while other passengers have their risk exposure evaluated. The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers suspected of having cases of hantavirus on board, leaves Praia, Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. Reuters Public health experts said they expected a more robust response from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health. "CDC would typically be asked by WHO to, or by a country to, help in technical assistance," Dr. Carlos del Rio, an H. Cliff Sauls distinguished professor of medicine at the Emory University School of Medicine, told reporters on Thursday. Typically, CDC teams would be deployed to an area, he said, and the teams would perform contact tracing and interviews and conduct an outbreak investigation. "I would envision by now, many, many days ago, we would have seen ... a team from CDC deployed to the area," he added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the IDSA, added that she would have expected a CDC press briefing, an alert from the agency's Health Alert Network or information from the NIH on potential treatments in the pipeline that could receive emergency use authorization to help treat hantavirus patients. Marrazzo said she is not aware that conversations about potential therapies at NIH aren't happening but it "does not give me a lot of assurance or reassurance that we're not hearing about any of it." The CDC posted a statement on X on Wednesday on behalf of NIH Director and acting CDC director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that read, "Our hearts go out to the passengers aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius and their families during this difficult time. Our CDC team began coordinating with domestic and international partners as soon as we were notified of a hantavirus situation." The statement said there is "clear, written health guidance to the American passengers through the State Department" and that the CDC "will continue to update as more information becomes available and remains committed to protecting the health and safety of the American public." The agency also published a statement on its website stating that the Trump administration "is closely monitoring the situation" and that the Department of State "is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." The CDC also said the risk to the American public is "extremely low." The WHO said during Thursday's press briefing that the U.S. is coordinating with the global health agency in a technical capacity. Because the cluster is limited and confined to a cruise ship, the "idea of sending messages across the world and panicking everyone is not required," said Dr. Abdirahman Mahmoud, director of the WHO's health emergency alert and response operations. He added that the WHO is "informally" aware that contact tracing has been done of the U.S. passengers who disembarked last month and are back home. news.content_title: Cryo-EM and AI-Designed Scaffold Reveal How Andes Hantavirus Binds Cells
news.content: Hantavirus [quantic69 / iStock / Getty Images Plus] Hantaviruses can turn exposure to infected rodents into a life-threatening illness, including a pulmonary syndrome that can progress rapidly to respiratory failure. Andes virus adds another concern: unlike other hantaviruses known to cause human disease, it can also spread between people. Understanding how it first attaches to human cells could help researchers identify ways to interrupt infection. Researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, Institut Pasteur in Paris, and LSU Health Shreveport have now resolved that interaction in near-atomic detail. Combining cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and functional experiments, they showed how the Andes virus spike captures a human receptor—and how antibodies interfere. The study, published in Nature , is titled “ Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses .” Previous research established that Andes virus and other New World hantaviruses use the cell-surface protein protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells. What remained unclear was how the viral spike recognized this receptor. An isolated spike subunit could not bind PCDH1; the interaction required the assembled, four-part structure. To examine that assembly, the team engineered a soluble Andes virus spike using methods that included an artificial intelligence–designed scaffold. The scaffold helped stabilize the square-shaped complex outside the virus, allowing the researchers to combine it with PCDH1 and analyze the resulting structure using cryo-EM. rVSV-ANDV infected cells (green) and PCDH1 bound to them (pink) [Albert Einstein College of Medicine] The images revealed that PCDH1 binds asymmetrically within a deep central pocket formed by four copies of the viral Gn glycoprotein. Rather than presenting a receptor-binding site on an individual subunit, the spike builds one through the arrangement of its components. Mutagenesis experiments identified three Gn loops that help shape the binding site. Changes involving these loops also enabled the researchers to transfer PCDH1-binding ability from New World to Old World hantavirus glycoproteins, according to the paper. The team also investigated four neutralizing antibodies. Structural and functional analyses showed that the antibodies prevented receptor binding through two mechanisms: obstructing access to the PCDH1-binding site or creating a physical barrier that prevented receptor engagement. “The depth of this pocket also helps explain how the virus limits antibody access. What’s striking is how the same pocket can accommodate the receptor while restricting antibody access. PCDH1’s long, slender shape lets it reach deep inside, but most antibodies are too bulky to follow,” said Rohit Jangra, PhD, assistant professor of microbiology and immunology at LSU Health Shreveport. That distinction suggests a direction for therapeutic development. According to the researchers, engineered molecules with a narrow, elongated shape might reach farther into the pocket and block attachment. The team intends to explore this vulnerability as a basis for antiviral strategies against Andes virus and potentially related pathogens, including Sin Nombre virus. The authors wrote, “Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.” News

news.content_original: Hantavirus [quantic69 / iStock / Getty Images Plus] Hantaviruses can turn exposure to infected rodents into a life-threatening illness, including a pulmonary syndrome that can progress rapidly to respiratory failure. Understanding how it first attaches to human cells could help researchers identify ways to interrupt infection. To examine that assembly, the team engineered a soluble Andes virus spike using methods that included an artificial intelligence–designed scaffold. What’s striking is how the same pocket can accommodate the receptor while restricting antibody access. PCDH1’s long, slender shape lets it reach deep inside, but most antibodies are too bulky to follow,” said Rohit Jangra, PhD, assistant professor of microbiology and immunology at LSU Health Shreveport. According to the researchers, engineered molecules with a narrow, elongated shape might reach farther into the pocket and block attachment. news.content: 24/7 LiveLos AngelesOrange CountyInland EmpireVentura CountyCalifornia 67° HEALTH & FITNESS Confirmed hantavirus cases linked to suspected cluster rises to 5, WHO says Swiss authorities also confirmed a case in a passenger who had left the ship. The total number of hantavirus cases in the suspected outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius has risen to five. ByZoe Magee and Dragana Jovanovic Wednesday, May 6, 2026 Share Follow ABC7 on Google The total number of hantavirus cases in the suspected outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius has risen to five, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The two new confirmed cases are among people who were medically evacuated from the ship earlier on Wednesday and are said to be in "serious" condition. The two patients and a third person, who is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2, were going to be transferred to ambulances waiting on the shore to receive them, WHO officials in Cape Verde told ABC News. They would then be taken to an airport, where they were expected to board a special medical evacuation flight to the Netherlands. "WHO continues to work with the ship's operators to closely monitor the health of passengers and crew, working with countries to support appropriate medical follow-up and evacuation where needed," Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO, said in a post on X on Wednesday, in which he confirmed the evacuations. "Monitoring and follow-up for passengers on board and for those who have already disembarked has been initiated in collaboration with the ship's operators and national health authorities," he continued. Tedros added that "the overall public health risk remains low." The three previously confirmed hantavirus cases include a woman who disembarked and was on her way home from the Netherlands, a British national who is in critical but stable condition in a hospital in Johannesburg, and a passenger who traveled on the first leg of the voyage and is currently being treated at the University Hospital Zurich, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the ship. So far, three deaths have been recorded. "Swiss authorities have confirmed a case of hantavirus identified in a passenger from the MV Hondius cruise ship," the WHO said on X on Wednesday. "He had responded to an email from the ship's operator informing the passengers of the health event, and presented himself to a hospital in Zurich, Switzerland, and is receiving care." An epidemiologist at the WHO also said on Wednesday that there may be some person-to-person spread in the outbreak. The type of virus in this outbreak has been confirmed as Andes hantavirus by the the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in South Africa and Geneva University Hospitals in Switzerland, the WHO said Wednesday. The Andes hantavirus historically has been shown to potentially transmit between people, according to the WHO. Oceanwide Expeditions said of the three passengers who were evacuated from the ship, two are symptomatic and in serious condition and the third is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2. This ensures that optimal medical care can be provided if necessary, during the next stage of this evolving situation," the company said in a statement. The ship departed Cape Verde with nearly 150 people on board and headed to Spain's Canary Islands, where Spanish health authorities will take over further investigations, including lab testing and clinical assessments, particularly for older passengers. The president of the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the northwestern coast of Africa, said on Wednesday that the regional government was opposed to allowing the luxury cruise ship to dock in Tenerife. "This decision is not based on any technical criteria, nor is there sufficient information to reassure the public or guarantee their safety," President Fernando Clavijo told radio station COPE, according to Reuters. Clavijo said on social media that he had requested a meeting with the Spanish prime minister to discuss the ship. He added that the Canary Islands "always acts with responsibility, but it cannot accept decisions taken behind the backs of the Canary Islands institutions and without sufficient information to the population." Mónica García, Spain's minister of health, said once the ship arrives at the port of Granadilla de Abona in the Canary Islands, there will be a "joint screening and evacuation mechanism will be launched to repatriate all passengers," according to RTVE, a Spanish national public broadcaster. "Unless their medical condition prevents it, all foreign passengers will be repatriated through the European civil protection mechanism, about which the Interior Minister will provide further details later," Garcia said in Spanish. WHO officials earlier on Wednesday said the three evacuated people were to be transferred to planes bound for both the Netherlands and Tenerife, but later updated the plan so that all would be sent to the Netherlands, officials told ABC News. analysis.brief_en: A suspected hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius has seen the number of confirmed cases rise to five, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The outbreak, linked to the Andes hantavirus, has resulted in three deaths, with two patients in serious condition and one asymptomatic close contact. The ship, which departed Cape Verde on May 6, 2026, is heading to Spain's Canary Islands, where further investigations will be conducted. WHO officials have confirmed that the overall public health risk remains low, but there may be some person-to-person transmission. In response, two infectious disease physicians from the Netherlands have joined the ship to provide medical care. The Canary Islands government has decided against allowing the ship to dock in Tenerife, citing insufficient information and public safety concerns. The WHO continues to monitor the situation and support medical follow-up and evacuation as needed.

elements_zh.location_and_population: 疑似暴发事件发生在MV Hondius号游轮上,该游轮从佛得角出发,前往西班牙加那利群岛。受影响的人群包括乘客和机组人员,特别是老年人,因为他们患重病的风险较高。

elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 世卫组织官员正在与船舶运营商和国家卫生当局合作,监测乘客和船员的健康状况。两名来自荷兰的传染病医生已抵达船上提供最佳医疗护理。加那利群岛政府以信息不足和公共安全问题为由,决定不允许该船停靠在特内里费岛。

OffOn Stream on What to know about Nebraska's National Quarantine Unit as it prepares to bring in hantavirus cruise ship passengers The unit opened months before the COVID-19 pandemic hit. ByIvan Pereira and Mary Kekatos May 8, 2026, 10:01 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google One of America's most state-of-the-art quarantine centers is preparing to take in the U.S. passengers who were aboard the M/V Hondius cruise ship at the center of a hantavirus outbreak. Administrators of the National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, Nebraska, say they are ready to help the 17 American passengers stay safe. During a press briefing Friday, the officials likened the quarantine to a hotel stay and said there is not yet a defined period for how long the passengers would remain at the unit. "From the moment that the outbreak on the ship was announced last weekend, we have been working closely with our partners," Dr. John Lowe, the University of Nebraska Medical Center's director of the Global Center for Health Security, told reporters Friday. In this undated file photo, the Davis Global Center is shown in Omaha, Nebraska. UNMC and Nebraska Medicine As of Friday, no U.S. passenger aboard the M/V Hondius has confirmed hantavirus cases, though several state health officials said they are monitoring their residents who were in contact with some of those who were infected. According to the cruise ship operator, there are 17 Americans aboard the ship. Related Hantavirus live updates The National Quarantine Unit, managed by Nebraska Medicine and the University of Nebraska Medical Center is the only federally funded quarantine unit in the U.S. It opened in November 2019, just months before the COVID-19 pandemic, and the facility's services were designed to handle highly contagious breakouts. The unit was created by a previous $20 million grant from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response. In this screen grab from a video, a hallway at the National Quarantine Unit is shown at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, Nebraska. University of Nebraska Medical Center The 20-bed facility contains individual negative air pressure systems to safely house individuals exposed to highly hazardous communicable diseases, according to Nebraska Medicine and UNMC. Lowe told reporters that the 17 passengers will not need to be transported by EMS teams if they continue to show no symptoms before their arrival. "We don't expect to see any of these passengers transported off on a gurney. They're going to walk off a plane and walk into a vehicle and get driven over here and head into their quarantine room," he said. The quarantine period will be determined upon their arrival followed by an epidemiological investigation, leaders of the facility said. “At this point we don't have a defined quarantine period,” Lowe said. In this screen grab from a video, a room at the National Quarantine Unit is shown at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, Nebraska. University of Nebraska Medical Center "It's pretty much like living in a hotel room with delivery of food. They can use their exercise devices in the room, we do daily symptom and monitoring as well as vital sign checks," he said. Related How Argentina kept the hantavirus at bay during a 2019 outbreak The unit also contains a six-bed national biocontainment training center, which includes "a simulated biocontainment unit for advanced experiential training." "This high-fidelity simulation center includes a mock lab and autoclave," Nebraska Medicine and UNMC said. Nebraska Medicine and UNMC said the facility is staffed with an all-volunteer team "comprised of highly skilled nurses, physicians, and allied health professionals who complete quarterly training in specialized infection prevention and control processes as well as participate in exercises and drills." In this screen grab from a video, a room at the National Quarantine Unit is shown at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, Nebraska. University of Nebraska Medical Center The medical facility is also home to the Nebraska Biocontainment Unit, a which is designed to care for patients with "high-consequence infectious diseases." In this screen grab from Google Maps Street View, the Davis Global Center is shown in Omaha, Nebraska. Google Maps Street View "Should they develop symptoms and concerning that diagnosis we will assess them and take care of them in the bio containment unit," Dr. Angela Hewlett, the director of the biocontainment unit, told reporters. Hewlett stressed the public that the current situation with the virus is different than the COVID-19 pandemic. She noted that while there are a lot of unknowns about this outbreak, the Andes strain of the hantavirus is generally thought to spread only with very close contact with another individual. "You really need to be up close and personal with somebody," she told reporters. news.source_body_en: The National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, Nebraska, is preparing to receive 17 American passengers from the M/V Hondius cruise ship, which was involved in a hantavirus outbreak. The unit, which opened in November 2019, is designed to handle highly contagious diseases and includes individual negative air pressure systems for safety. While no confirmed hantavirus cases have been reported among the passengers, state health officials are monitoring those who had contact with infected individuals. The quarantine duration will be determined upon arrival, and the facility is staffed with an all-volunteer team trained in specialized infection prevention. Officials have likened the quarantine to a hotel stay, emphasizing that the passengers will have freedom during their stay, including the ability to make calls and use exercise equipment. The situation is under investigation, with daily symptom and vital sign monitoring in place.
