OffOn Stream on News Can I get hantavirus from my pet? Here's what pet owners should know Global race to contain hantavirus outbreak ByDr. Geraldine Nabeta May 14, 2026, 10:25 PM The recent headlines about illnesses and deaths tied to possible hantavirus exposure have left some pet owners wondering whether the virus can be spread through the furry creature sleeping on their couch or curled up on their lap. While cats and dogs can be infected with the hantavirus, they generally don’t have symptoms and experts say they are highly unlikely to infect their owners. Related Passenger from hantavirus-stricken cruise ship speaks out from quarantine "They can be exposed, but they don't get sick the way that we know people to get sick," Dr. Kate Elden, the chief medical officer of the veterinary telehealth company, Dutch, told ABC News. "There's no actual test that a veterinarian or your local vet is going to have." And even when a dog or cat does have a hantavirus infection, they don’t transfer the virus to humans, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. However, if they bring an infected wild rodent into the home that could theoretically increase your exposure, Elden cautioned. Stock photo of a dog and cat being fed. Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images "Don't hesitate to call your vet if your pet brought a rodent home and starts to [look] unwell," she said. Elden advised disposing of any rodent your pet has brought home while wearing a mask and gloves, and then thoroughly washing hands with soap and water after it has safely been dispatched. Even owners of pet rats and mice don’t have much to worry about, Elden said. "The domestic hamster, guinea pig, gerbil, these are captive bred animals, we have no documentation that they play a role in hantavirus cases or are part of spreading the disease," Elden said. To be safe, clean cages away from food preparation and spray down bedding to minimize dust particles in the air if necessary, she advised. Popular Reads Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search 1 day ago Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress 1 day ago Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Oct 16 Deer mice are the most likely natural hosts for hantavirus, the CDC notes. Related American who survived hantavirus in 1993 outbreak describes her symptoms and recovery The virus lives in their bodies without making them sick, and they spread it through their urine, droppings and saliva, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association. But your risk depends a lot on where you live. Hantavirus remain rare and scattered in the U.S., according to the CDC, with most cases reported in California, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. People typically become infected after inhaling contaminated particles, usually while cleaning sheds, cabins, garages or rodent-infested areas or while doing outdoor activities like hunting and camping. One rare exception is the Andes virus, a strain found mainly in South America that can spread from person to person through close contact and has been linked to the recent cruise ship cases. Pets are not known to spread Andes virus to humans. The CDC lists early symptoms of hantavirus similar to those resembling the flu, including fever, muscle aches, fatigue, headache, nausea and shortness of breath. The infection can quickly take a turn, becoming more severe and affecting the lungs. Related Former White House COVID-19 response coordinator answers hantavirus questions The best way to avoid infection is by reducing rodent activity near your home, Elden said. Seal any holes and clean rodent droppings with a disinfectant instead of sweeping or vacuuming. Keep pet food sealed. And if you think you've been exposed through any source, the CDC recommends seeking immediate medical attention. Geraldine Nabeta MD MSc is an incoming chief resident in internal medicine at the University of Connecticut and a member of the ABC News Medical Unit. analysis.brief_en: This article from ABC News addresses concerns among pet owners about the possibility of contracting hantavirus from their pets. Experts clarify that while cats and dogs can be infected with hantavirus, they typically do not show symptoms and are highly unlikely to transmit the virus to humans. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) emphasizes that hantavirus is primarily spread through rodent excretions, and pets are not known to spread the Andes virus, a rare strain linked to recent cruise ship cases. The CDC advises reducing rodent activity near homes, sealing holes, and cleaning droppings with disinfectant instead of sweeping or vacuuming. It also recommends seeking immediate medical attention if exposure is suspected. The article notes that hantavirus remains rare in the U.S., with most cases reported in specific states. Pet owners are encouraged to clean cages away from food preparation and minimize dust particles in the air if necessary. The article highlights that domesticated animals like hamsters, guinea pigs, and gerbils are not known to spread hantavirus, as they are captive-bred and not natural hosts. Overall, the risk of transmission from pets is considered low, but vigilance against rodents is advised.

news.content_zh: ABC 新闻的这篇文章解决了宠物主人对其宠物感染汉坦病毒的可能性的担忧。专家澄清,虽然猫和狗可能感染 汉坦病毒,但它们通常不会表现出症状,并且极不可能将病毒传播给人类。美国疾病控制与预防中心 (CDC) 强调,汉坦病毒 主要通过啮齿类动物的排泄物传播,目前还不知道宠物会传播安第斯病毒,这是一种与最近的游轮病例有关的罕见病毒。疾病预防控制中心建议减少房屋附近的啮齿动物活动,密封洞口,并用消毒剂清洁粪便,而不是清扫或吸尘。它还建议如果怀疑接触,立即就医。文章指出,汉坦病毒 在美国仍然很少见,大多数病例都是在特定州报告的。鼓励宠物主人清洁笼子,使其远离准备食物的地方,并在必要时尽量减少空气中的灰尘颗粒。文章强调,仓鼠、豚鼠和沙鼠等家养动物不会传播 汉坦病毒,因为它们是人工饲养的,而不是天然的 宿主。总体而言,宠物感染 传播 的风险较低,但建议对啮齿动物保持警惕。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology From Viral Entry to Genome Replication: Mapping the Druggable Weak Points of Hantaviruses by October 17, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 From Viral Entry to Genome Replication: Mapping the Druggable Weak Points of Hantaviruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Orthohantaviruses, rodent-borne enveloped viruses with tri-segmented single-stranded negative-sense RNA genomes, remain among the most dangerous yet therapeutically neglected human pathogens. They cause two life-threatening clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas, the latter carrying case fatality rates that can approach or exceed 50 percent. Despite decades of research and recurring outbreaks, including a highly publicized Andes virus outbreak aboard a cruise ship in April 2026, there is still no universally licensed antiviral or vaccine against orthohantavirus infection. A recent review published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology by researchers at the University of São Paulo and Institut Pasteur de São Paulo systematically maps the viral life cycle for chemotherapeutic intervention, evaluating entry inhibitors, polymerase blockers, nucleocapsid disruptors, and host-directed strategies while advocating for computational approaches to accelerate discovery. The authors frame their analysis around the fundamental steps of the orthohantavirus infection cycle. Viral entry begins when the Gn glycoprotein docks onto host surface receptors, including β3-integrins and protocadherin-1 (PCDH1). Once internalized via endocytosis, the acidification of the endosomal compartment triggers a conformational change in the viral envelope that drives membrane fusion, releasing the viral genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) then initiates both transcription and genome replication. Structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA genomes assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane before budding out as mature infectious virions. Each of these stages presents a distinct molecular vulnerability that chemists and virologists can exploit with rationally designed small molecules, peptides, or biologics. Among the most extensively characterized entry inhibitors are cyclic peptides identified through phage display libraries. Early work identified cyclic nonapeptides that bind the β3-integrin receptor used by pathogenic orthohantaviruses such as Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) to enter human endothelial cells. Of seventy sequences screened, eleven showed inhibitory effects exceeding 80 percent against SNV in vitro, with the most potent, CPFVKTQLC, demonstrating high inhibitory potency when presented on phage particles. This peptide was subsequently refined through alanine substitution and deletion scanning to a minimal functional unit, the cyclic pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC]. However, because free monovalent peptides proved less effective than phage-displayed versions, researchers pivoted toward multivalent presentation on nanoparticles, targeting the viral glycoproteins directly rather than the host receptor. When the peptide CLVRNLAWC was displayed on 100-nanometer nanoparticles at a 4:1 ratio, inhibition of SNV rose from 9 percent as a free peptide to 32.5 percent. The peptide CQATTARNC achieved even greater efficacy, surpassing 50 percent inhibition when the nanoparticle-to-virus ratio was increased to 20:1. Building on these strategies, investigators extended the approach to Andes virus (ANDV) by eluting peptide libraries from purified virions using monoclonal antibodies against the Gn and Gc glycoproteins. A key finding was that combining peptides targeting different Gn- and Gc-specific sequences produced synergistic inhibition significantly more powerful than single-peptide treatments, underscoring the value of simultaneously engaging multiple viral epitopes. To transition from biological peptides to drug-like molecules, researchers used the three-dimensional structure of the refined pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC] in a ligand-based virtual screening campaign evaluating over 600,000 small molecules. This effort identified compounds such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which were approximately 2,000 times more potent than the original cyclic peptides, achieving high-affinity inhibition in the nanomolar range with EC50 values between 1.3 and 2.5 nanomolar in vitro. These molecules represent a compelling proof of concept that computational screening can transform a modest peptide lead into a highly potent preclinical candidate warranting further in vivo evaluation. A distinct strategy targets the membrane fusion process itself. The orthohantavirus Gc glycoprotein functions as a class II fusion protein, and completing membrane fusion requires a major structural relocation of Domain III (DIII) to achieve the post-fusion state. Exploiting this mechanical vulnerability, researchers demonstrated that viral entry can be blocked using recombinant fragments and synthetic peptides derived from the Gc DIII and stem region. These fragments allow initial Gc trimerization to proceed but ultimately prevent membrane hemifusion and fusion pore formation. The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by approximately 70 percent at 25 micromolar and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50 percent. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal portion of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95 percent in vitro. Although efficacy dropped to a 70 percent cross-reduction against PUUV-mediated fusion at 20 micromolar due to high genetic divergence between the two viruses, the results still demonstrate meaningful cross-protective potential. Natural products have also yielded promising entry inhibitors. Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin with demonstrated efficacy against coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and herpesviruses, potently inhibits ANDV entry in vitro. A synthetic trimeric variant possessing nine oligosaccharide-binding sites showed even greater potency against ANDV and SNV. In vivo, GRFT inhibited HTNV and provided partial protection in suckling mice. Its scalability and ease of purification highlight its translational potential. Separately, bovine lactoferrin (LF) prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion of SEOV, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin or by sterically hindering virus binding to host β-integrin and lectin receptors. Prophylactic administration of LF one day before orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70 percent at 160 milligrams per kilogram, with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94 percent. When combined with subsequent ribavirin treatment, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shedding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression. Discovered through high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus with an EC50 of 0.9 micromolar and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73 percent at 20 micromolar. In vivo, administration to BALB/c mice five hours post-infection significantly reduced infection by 93 percent at 90 milligrams per kilogram per day and 94 percent at 180 milligrams per kilogram per day. Given its established safety profile, CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses. On the replication front, ribavirin remains the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy. Once transported into host cells, ribavirin is phosphorylated into metabolites including ribavirin-5′-monophosphate, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and depletes intracellular GTP, and ribavirin-5′-triphosphate, which selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action. Incorporation of ribavirin leads to accumulation of genomic errors and dramatic loss of virus viability through error catastrophe. Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early ribavirin administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with HTNV and hamster models infected with ANDV. Clinically, intravenous ribavirin demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, significantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality. However, efficacy varies significantly across strains and clinical syndromes. In the context of HCPS caused by ANDV, ribavirin intervention eliminated mortality compared to a 35 percent historical case-fatality rate and reduced the incidence of the severe cardiopulmonary phase from 84 to 57 percent. Conversely, in a larger placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial evaluating intravenous ribavirin for HCPS, the drug failed to demonstrate overall therapeutic efficacy, revealing no significant difference in survival between groups. Trials in HFRS caused by PUUV also showed insufficient efficacy and safety, likely due to delayed drug administration and a weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection. Furthermore, the clinical utility of ribavirin is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia reported in 71 percent of recipients. Favipiravir (T-705), originally discovered during a screening for anti-influenza compounds, has emerged as a potent viral replication inhibitor. Upon cellular entry, host enzymes convert favipiravir into its active form, favipiravir-RTP, a purine nucleotide analogue incorporated into nascent viral RNA that induces lethal mutagenesis. Favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro and provided 100 percent survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. Combination with ribavirin produced highly synergistic effects, with peak antiviral activity observed at a ratio of 12 micromolar favipiravir to 18.75 micromolar ribavirin, achieving greater than 99 percent overall inhibition of HTNV. Additionally, ETAR (1-β-D-ribofuranosyl-3-ethynyl-[1,2,4]triazole) demonstrated high potency in vitro against HTNV and ANDV, and in vivo studies using HTNV-challenged suckling mice showed approximately 25 percent protection at doses of just 12.5 and 25 milligrams per kilogram, mirroring ribavirin’s therapeutic outcomes at a fraction of the concentration. Beyond nucleoside analogues, the viral nucleoprotein has emerged as a promising alternative target. Terpene-isoindole conjugates such as compound 18 demonstrated potent anti-HTNV activity with exceptionally low toxicity, and molecular docking suggests they bind to the highly conserved RNA-binding site of the nucleoprotein, competing with viral RNA and effectively arresting intracellular replication. Similarly, morin, a natural flavonoid found in plants like mulberry and perilla, binds directly to the core assembly region of the viral nucleoprotein, sterically hindering RNA encapsidation and disrupting the formation of functional replication complexes. In the absence of licensed antiviral treatments, clinical management remains primarily supportive, focusing on intensive monitoring and treatment of respiratory, cardiac, and renal complications. Achieving early diagnosis remains a primary clinical challenge, as the efficacy of supportive care is substantially reduced if initiated after the onset of severe disease. Host-targeted and anti-inflammatory strategies have recently been explored to mitigate the characteristic vascular leak and cytokine storm, most notably during the 2026 cruise ship outbreak, where the JAK inhibitor baricitinib and the bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist icatibant were administered in a combined therapeutic regimen alongside ribavirin and favipiravir. Passive immunotherapy continues to be a major investigative focus, with convalescent plasma showing potential to reduce mortality and newer candidates such as the quadrivalent human polyclonal antibody SAB-163 and highly potent monoclonal antibodies demonstrating up to 100 percent protection in lethal animal models. Regarding prevention, Hantavax has been used to prevent HFRS in South Korea, and China routinely administers inactivated bivalent vaccines targeting HTNV and SEOV in endemic regions. However, a globally licensed orthohantavirus vaccine does not currently exist, leaving New World strains and HCPS without an approved preventative countermeasure. The review’s authors argue that expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants, combined with modern in silico screening of extensive chemical and natural product libraries, will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats. The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by approximately 70 percent at 25 micromolar and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50 percent. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal portion of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95 percent in vitro. Although efficacy dropped to a 70 percent cross-reduction against PUUV-mediated fusion at 20 micromolar due to high genetic divergence between the two viruses, the results still demonstrate meaningful cross-protective potential. Natural products have also yielded promising entry inhibitors. Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin with demonstrated efficacy against coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and herpesviruses, potently inhibits ANDV entry in vitro. A synthetic trimeric variant possessing nine oligosaccharide-binding sites showed even greater potency against ANDV and SNV. In vivo, GRFT inhibited HTNV and provided partial protection in suckling mice. Its scalability and ease of purification highlight its translational potential. Separately, bovine lactoferrin (LF) prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion of SEOV, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin or by sterically hindering virus binding to host β-integrin and lectin receptors. Prophylactic administration of LF one day before orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70 percent at 160 milligrams per kilogram, with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94 percent. When combined with subsequent ribavirin treatment, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shedding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression. Discovered through high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus with an EC50 of 0.9 micromolar and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73 percent at 20 micromolar. In vivo, administration to BALB/c mice five hours post-infection significantly reduced infection by 93 percent at 90 milligrams per kilogram per day and 94 percent at 180 milligrams per kilogram per day. Given its established safety profile, CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses. On the replication front, ribavirin remains the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy. Once transported into host cells, ribavirin is phosphorylated into metabolites including ribavirin-5′-monophosphate, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and depletes intracellular GTP, and ribavirin-5′-triphosphate, which selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action. Incorporation of ribavirin leads to accumulation of genomic errors and dramatic loss of virus viability through error catastrophe. Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early ribavirin administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with HTNV and hamster models infected with ANDV. Clinically, intravenous ribavirin demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, significantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality. However, efficacy varies significantly across strains and clinical syndromes. In the context of HCPS caused by ANDV, ribavirin intervention eliminated mortality compared to a 35 percent historical case-fatality rate and reduced the incidence of the severe cardiopulmonary phase from 84 to 57 percent. Conversely, in a larger placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial evaluating intravenous ribavirin for HCPS, the drug failed to demonstrate overall therapeutic efficacy, revealing no significant difference in survival between groups. Trials in HFRS caused by PUUV also showed insufficient efficacy and safety, likely due to delayed drug administration and a weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection. Furthermore, the clinical utility of ribavirin is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia reported in 71 percent of recipients. Favipiravir (T-705), originally discovered during a screening for anti-influenza compounds, has emerged as a potent viral replication inhibitor. Upon cellular entry, host enzymes convert favipiravir into its active form, favipiravir-RTP, a purine nucleotide analogue incorporated into nascent viral RNA that induces lethal mutagenesis. Favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro and provided 100 percent survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. Combination with ribavirin produced highly synergistic effects, with peak antiviral activity observed at a ratio of 12 micromolar favipiravir to 18.75 micromolar ribavirin, achieving greater than 99 percent overall inhibition of HTNV. Additionally, ETAR (1-β-D-ribofuranosyl-3-ethynyl-[1,2,4]triazole) demonstrated high potency in vitro against HTNV and ANDV, and in vivo studies using HTNV-challenged suckling mice showed approximately 25 percent protection at doses of just 12.5 and 25 milligrams per kilogram, mirroring ribavirin’s therapeutic outcomes at a fraction of the concentration. Beyond nucleoside analogues, the viral nucleoprotein has emerged as a promising alternative target. Terpene-isoindole conjugates such as compound 18 demonstrated potent anti-HTNV activity with exceptionally low toxicity, and molecular docking suggests they bind to the highly conserved RNA-binding site of the nucleoprotein, competing with viral RNA and effectively arresting intracellular replication. Similarly, morin, a natural flavonoid found in plants like mulberry and perilla, binds directly to the core assembly region of the viral nucleoprotein, sterically hindering RNA encapsidation and disrupting the formation of functional replication complexes. In the absence of licensed antiviral treatments, clinical management remains primarily supportive, focusing on intensive monitoring and treatment of respiratory, cardiac, and renal complications. Achieving early diagnosis remains a primary clinical challenge, as the efficacy of supportive care is substantially reduced if initiated after the onset of severe disease. Host-targeted and anti-inflammatory strategies have recently been explored to mitigate the characteristic vascular leak and cytokine storm, most notably during the 2026 cruise ship outbreak, where the JAK inhibitor baricitinib and the bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist icatibant were administered in a combined therapeutic regimen alongside ribavirin and favipiravir. Passive immunotherapy continues to be a major investigative focus, with convalescent plasma showing potential to reduce mortality and newer candidates such as the quadrivalent human polyclonal antibody SAB-163 and highly potent monoclonal antibodies demonstrating up to 100 percent protection in lethal animal models. Regarding prevention, Hantavax has been used to prevent HFRS in South Korea, and China routinely administers inactivated bivalent vaccines targeting HTNV and SEOV in endemic regions. However, a globally licensed orthohantavirus vaccine does not currently exist, leaving New World strains and HCPS without an approved preventative countermeasure. The review’s authors argue that expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants, combined with modern in silico screening of extensive chemical and natural product libraries, will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats. analysis.event: A review published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology by researchers at the University of São Paulo and Institut Pasteur de São Paulo systematically maps the viral life cycle for chemotherapeutic intervention, evaluating entry inhibitors, polymerase blockers, nucleocapsid disruptors, and host-directed strategies while advocating for computational approaches to accelerate discovery.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Hantaviruses cause two life-threatening clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas, with the latter having case fatality rates that can approach or exceed 50 percent. There is still no universally licensed antiviral or vaccine against orthohantavirus infection.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study outlines strategies for targeting different stages of the orthohantavirus infection cycle, including entry inhibitors, polymerase blockers, and host-directed approaches. It highlights the potential of computational screening to identify potent drug candidates, such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which showed high-affinity inhibition in the nanomolar range. The research also discusses the use of natural products and favipiravir as entry and replication inhibitors, with favipiravir showing 100 percent survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia.

analysis.brief_en: This news report discusses a recent study published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology, which focuses on mapping the druggable weak points of hantaviruses. The research, conducted by scientists at the University of São Paulo and Institut Pasteur de São Paulo, evaluates various strategies to target the viral life cycle, including entry inhibitors, polymerase blockers, and host-directed approaches. Hantaviruses are known to cause two severe clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas, with HCPS having fatality rates that can exceed 50 percent. Despite ongoing research and outbreaks, such as the Andes virus incident on a cruise ship in April 2026, there is currently no universally licensed antiviral or vaccine. The study highlights the potential of computational screening to identify potent drug candidates, such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which demonstrated high-affinity inhibition in the nanomolar range. Additionally, the research explores the use of natural products and favipiravir as entry and replication inhibitors, with favipiravir showing promising results in hamster models of ANDV infection, achieving 100 percent survival when administered before viremia. The findings suggest that these approaches could lead to the development of effective treatments for hantavirus infections.
